# Tobit Chapter 10 — Disagreement Log
**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Date:** 2026-03-17

## Overview
Chapter 10 is the chapter of waiting, grief, and farewell. It produced 12 significant divergences across 13 verses, most concentrated in Anna's grief sequence (vv. 1-6) and the parting speeches (vv. 10-12). The central tension across all three agents is between emotional directness and textual fidelity — PNEUMA repeatedly reaches for modern idioms that intensify the feeling but depart from the Greek; EMET stays close at the cost of naturalness; LOGOS finds the middle.

---

## Disagreement Table

| Verse | Issue | EMET | LOGOS | PNEUMA | SOPHIA Resolution |
|-------|-------|------|-------|--------|-------------------|
| 10:1 | Opening orientation | No temporal marker | "Meanwhile" | "Back home" | "Meanwhile" — LOGOS; necessary for reader orientation at chapter break |
| 10:3 | Personal pronoun in Anna's cry | "The boy" | "My boy" | "Our boy" | "My boy" — Greek has ho pais mou (my child/my boy); "Our" is PNEUMA's addition |
| 10:3 | Grief idiom | "was grieved in-soul" | "grew heavy with grief" | "grief settled over him like a weight" | LOGOS: concise, bodily, natural |
| 10:4 | Exclamatory structure | Literal interjection "O woe to-me" | "Woe is me" | Restructured as question | "Woe is me" — LOGOS; preserves lament register |
| 10:5 | Tobit's command | "Be-silent!" | "Hush." | "Hush." | "Hush." — LOGOS/PNEUMA; sigaton rendered naturally |
| 10:6 | Anna's sharp reply | "Be-silent yourself!" | "Be silent yourself!" | "Don't tell me to be quiet" | LOGOS: formal enough for the narrative register |
| 10:7 | Length of Tobias's speech | Preserved fully | Preserved fully | Compressed | Preserved fully (EMET/LOGOS) — the petition's formal length is narratively important |
| 10:9 | Goods inventory | Full hyphenated itemization | Full natural itemization | Partially compressed | Full itemization (LOGOS style) — legal and social weight requires specificity |
| 10:10 | Raguel's physical gesture | "embraced" | "embraced" | "threw his arms around" | "embraced" — EMET/LOGOS; perilabon = "clasping/embracing," not a more dramatic gesture |
| 10:11 | Address form for Sarah | bare "daughter" | "my daughter" | "my darling girl" | "my daughter" — LOGOS adds the possessive naturally present in Greek; PNEUMA adds affection beyond the text |
| 10:12 | Scope of Edna's charge | "grief all the days of your life" | "grief all the days of your life" | "ever make her cry" | LOGOS: lupe is grief in the broad sense, not specifically crying |
| 10:13 | Closing sentence | Literal but awkward | Integrated | Paraphrased | Normalized LOGOS base with minor clarification |

---

## Extended Notes

### Anna's Grief (vv. 3-6)
This is among the most vivid portraits of maternal grief in ancient literature. The detail in verse 6 — that she ate but did not stop weeping at night — is unique to the Sinaiticus (GII) and psychologically acute. PNEUMA's instinct to dramatize is understandable here; but SOPHIA notes that the Greek itself is already dramatic, and the translator's job is to get out of its way.

PNEUMA's rendering of Anna's retort ("Don't tell me to be quiet. Don't try to fool me") is colloquial in a way that works emotionally but slides toward anachronism. LOGOS's "Be silent yourself! Do not deceive me" preserves the direct confrontation while keeping register.

### The Farewell Speeches (vv. 10-12)
Three separate farewells (Raguel to Tobias, Raguel to Sarah, Edna to Tobias) are given in rapid succession. All three agents recognized the structural parallelism. The key divergence is Edna's charge in verse 12: "Do not cause her grief all the days of your life." PNEUMA's "do not ever make her cry" is emotionally resonant but loses the breadth of the Greek lupe (grief, pain, sorrow — not only weeping). SOPHIA retains the fuller meaning.

### The cheirograph resolution
The money subplot, introduced in chapter 1 and resolved in chapter 9, is now complete. The inheritance transfer in verse 9 marks Tobias as legally a full member of Raguel's household — a new social identity that the inventory of goods formally confers.

*— SOPHIA*
